# Package loading

We start by importing the packages we will need to load and clean our datasets.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(here)
library(readxl)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(sf)
```

# Data import

We can now proceed to the loading of our datasets.

```{r}
#| message: false
here::i_am("Data Analysis Public Services.Rproj")
```

```{r}
#| message: false

pov15<-read_excel("Raw Datasets/2015_department_poverty_rate.xlsx",skip=5)
pov16<-read_excel("Raw Datasets/2016_department_poverty_rate.xlsx",skip=5)

pov20<-read_excel("Raw Datasets/2020_department_poverty_rate.xlsx",skip=5)

pov23<-read_excel("Raw Datasets/2023_department_poverty_rate.xlsx")
```

# Data cleaning

Now that we have our datasets loaded, we proceed to clean them so we have usable dataframes.

Because the poverty rate files are different from one year to another, we have to proceed case by case.

```{r}
# Poverty rates
pov15 <- pov15 |> 
  select("CODGEO","TP6015" ) |> 
  slice(-97,-98) |> 
  rename(dpt_id = 1, `2015` = 2)

pov16 <- pov16 |> 
  select("CODGEO","TP6016" ) |> 
  slice(-97,-98) |> 
  rename(dpt_id = 1, `2016` = 2)

pov17 <- pov17 |> 
  select("2. Taux de pauvreté en 2017","...3") |> 
  slice(-1,-(98:106)) |> 
  rename(dpt_id = 1, `2017` = 2)

pov18 <- pov18 |> 
  select("2. Taux de pauvreté par département en 2018","...3") |> 
  slice(-1,-2,-(99:106)) |> 
  rename(dpt_id = 1, `2018` = 2)

pov19 <- pov19 |> 
  select("CODGEO","TP6019" ) |> 
  slice(-(97:105)) |> 
  rename(dpt_id = 1, `2019` = 2)

pov20 <- pov20 |> 
  select("CODGEO","TP6020" ) |>
  slice(-(97:105)) |> 
  rename(dpt_id = 1, `2020` = 2)

pov21 <- pov21 |> 
  select("Figure 2 – Taux de pauvreté par département en 2021","...3") |> 
  slice(-1,-2,-(99:107)) |> 
  rename(dpt_id = 1, `2021` = 2)

pov23 <- pov23 |> 
  select(-"...2") |> 
  slice(-(1:3),-100) |> 
  rename(dpt_id = 1, `2023` = 2)
```

We now join all the annual poverty rates to get a longitudinal dataframe:

```{r}
pov_tot <- reduce(
  list(pov15, pov16, pov17, pov18, pov19, pov20, pov21, pov23),
  full_join,
  by = "dpt_id")

# The 2020 column had comas instead of dots, so we modify this
pov_tot <- pov_tot |>
  mutate(`2020` = as.double(gsub(",", ".", `2020`)))

# Then we convert all the dataframe to doubles
pov_tot <- pov_tot |>
  mutate(across(-dpt_id, as.double))

# Now that we have pov_tot, we don't need the annual dataframes
rm(pov15,pov16,pov17,pov18,pov19,pov20,pov21,pov23)
```

```{r}
# Unemployment rate
unemp_quart <- unemp_quart |>
  slice(-(97:104)) |>
  select(-"Libellé") |>
  rename(dpt_id = 1)

# We now want an annual unemployement rate instead of a quarterly one
unemp_tot <- unemp_quart |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -dpt_id,
    names_to = c("trimestre", "annee"),
    names_sep = "_",
    values_to = "taux") |> 
  group_by(dpt_id, annee) |>
  summarise(taux = mean(taux), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = annee, values_from = taux)

# Now that we have unemp_tot, we don't need the quarterly dataframe
rm(unemp_quart)

```

```{r}
# Social housing
housing <- housing |>
  slice(-(1:4)) |>
  select(-2) |>
  rename(dpt_id = 1) 

housing<-housing |>
  select(dpt_id, rev(setdiff(names(housing), "dpt_id"))) |>
  rename(`2015`=2,`2016`=3,`2017`=4,`2018`=5,`2019`=6,`2020`=7,`2021`=8,`2022`=9,`2023`=10,)|> 
  mutate(across(-dpt_id, as.numeric))

```

```{r}
#| output: false

#codes of the facilities we keep
codes_ok <- c("A10G", "A104", "A206", "A207", "A208")

#names of the different codes
labels <- tibble(
  FACILITY_TYPE = c("A10G", "A104", "A206", "A207", "A208"),
  facility_name = c("Public Finances", "National Gendarmerie", "Post Office",
                    "Post Office Relay", "Municipal Post Office")
)

#evolution dataset, departments
bpe_evol <- bpe_evol_raw |>
  filter(GEO_OBJECT == "DEP",
         !startsWith(GEO, "97"),
         FACILITY_TYPE %in% codes_ok) |>
  transmute(DPT_ID = GEO,
            FACILITY_TYPE,
            year = as.integer(TIME_PERIOD),
            nb = as.numeric(OBS_VALUE))

#we sum to have our data at department level, A120+A121=A10G
bpe_2021 <- bpe_2021_raw |>
  filter(!startsWith(DEP, "97")) |>
  mutate(NB_EQUIP = as.numeric(NB_EQUIP),
         FACILITY_TYPE = if_else(TYPEQU %in% c("A120", "A121"), "A10G", TYPEQU)) |>
  filter(FACILITY_TYPE %in% codes_ok) |>
  group_by(DPT_ID = DEP, FACILITY_TYPE) |>
  summarise(nb = sum(NB_EQUIP), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(year = 2021L)

#putting both data together
bpe_long <- bind_rows(bpe_evol, bpe_2021) |>
  complete(DPT_ID, FACILITY_TYPE, year, fill = list(nb = 0)) |>
  left_join(labels, by = "FACILITY_TYPE") |>
  arrange(FACILITY_TYPE, DPT_ID, year) |>
  rename(`Facility Code` = FACILITY_TYPE,
         `Facility Name` = facility_name)

#arranging to have 1 column per year
bpe_clean <- bpe_long |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = nb, names_sort = TRUE) |>
  select(DPT_ID, `Facility Code`, `Facility Name`, everything())

#saving
write_csv2(bpe_clean, "Clean Datasets/bpe_dep_wide.csv")
write_csv2(bpe_long, "Clean Datasets/bpe_dep_long.csv")
rm(bpe_evol, bpe_2021, labels)
```

```{r}
#| message: false
# Department boundaries (IGN Admin Express, simplified version)
ae_file   <- "Raw Datasets/adminexpress-cog-simpl-000-2026.gpkg"
dep_layer <- grep("^departement$", st_layers(ae_file)$name,
                  ignore.case = TRUE, value = TRUE)[1]
dep_raw   <- st_read(ae_file, layer = dep_layer, quiet = TRUE)
code_col  <- intersect(c("INSEE_DEP", "insee_dep", "code_insee", "CODE_INSEE"),
                       names(dep_raw))[1]

# Metropolitan departments only, Lambert-93 projection
dep_geo <- dep_raw |>
  select(dpt_id = all_of(code_col)) |>
  filter(dpt_id %in% pov_tot$dpt_id) |>
  st_transform(2154)

# Join with poverty rates and compute the 2015-2021 change
map_data <- dep_geo |>
  left_join(pov_tot |> select(dpt_id, `2015`, `2021`), by = "dpt_id") |>
  mutate(change = `2021` - `2015`,
         change_class = cut(change,
                            breaks = c(-Inf, -1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5, Inf),
                            labels = c("Strong decrease (< -1.5 pts)",
                                       "Decrease (-1.5 to -0.5 pts)",
                                       "Stable (-0.5 to +0.5 pts)",
                                       "Increase (+0.5 to +1.5 pts)",
                                       "Strong increase (> +1.5 pts)")))

rm(dep_raw)
```

## Description of the sources

Our data come from French public institutions, which publish official statistics under an open licence. Most files are produced by Insee, the "Institut National de la Statistique et des Etudes Economiques", which is responsible for collecting and publishing economic and social statistics. The others come from ministerial statistical services and from the open data platform data.gouv.fr.

Poverty rates (Insee). Poverty rates by departement come from Filosofi, a dataset built by Insee from tax records and social benefit data (provided by the tax administration and by family, pension and agricultural social security funds). The poverty rate is the share of the population whose standard of living is below 60% of the national median standard of living. It is expressed as a percentage.

Population per departement (Insee). Annual population estimates by departement, based on the population census and updated with demographic data. We use them to compute per-capita indicators and to compare departements of very different sizes.

Unemployment rate (Insee). Local unemployment rates by departement, based on the International Labour Organization definition. They combine the Labour Force Survey with administrative sources and are published quarterly.

Social housing (SDES, RPLS). The RPLS (Répertoire des logements locatifs des bailleurs sociaux) is an annual inventory of social rental housing, managed by the statistical service of the Ministry of Ecological Transition (SDES). It records housing owned by social landlords, so it measures the supply of social housing in each departement.

France Services structures (data.gouv.fr). A list of the “France Services” houses, one-stop shops that give residents access to several public services (tax, social benefits, employment, etc.) in one place. It gives the location of each structure and lets us measure access to public services.

Social minima (DREES). DREES is the statistical service of the Ministry of Health and Solidarity. We use two files on social minima by departement: one by benefit scheme, and one specifically on RSA (the minimum income benefit) and the “prime d’activité” (an in-work benefit). They show how many households depend on these benefits in each area.

BPE (Insee). The "Base permanente des équipements" is an annual geolocated database of facilities and services available to the population (shops, health, education, sports, transport, etc.). We use it to describe the local availability of services.

## Information about each data file

The dataframes obtained after the import and the cleaning are the ones we are going to use for our study. They are the following:

- `pov_tot`: Poverty rate per department and per year (2015-2023 but without 2022, because the data was not available for this year.)
- `unemp_tot`: Unemployment rate per department and per year (2015-2023)
- `housing`: Number of social housing units per department and per year (2015-2023)
- `AAH`, `ASPA`, `ASS`, `PPA`, `RSA`: Number of beneficiaries of each social minima (respectively Allocation aux adultes handicapés, Allocation de solidarité aux personnes âgées, Allocation de solidarité spécifique, Prime d’activité and Revenu de solidarité active), per department and per year (2015-2023 except for `RSA` and `PPA` that are 2016-2023 because they were combined in a single social minima before 2016.)
- `france_serv`: Number of France services houses per department and per year (2016-2023). Notice that they were implemented in 2020, so the values before 2020 are all zeros.
- `bpe_clean`: Number of structures of each facility type present in each department in the years 2015, 2020, 2021, 2025 (the BPE was not available for every year). The facility types we are interested in are: National Gendarmerie (A104), Public Finances (A10G), Post office (A206), Post office relay (A207), Municipal post office (A208).

We now implement a table for each dataframe, which contains its number of rows and number of columns:

| Number of rows of pov_tot | Number of columns of pov_tot |
|---------------------------|------------------------------|
| `r nrow(pov_tot)`         | `r ncol(pov_tot)`            |

| Number of rows of unemp_tot | Number of columns of unemp_tot |
|-----------------------------|--------------------------------|
| `r nrow(unemp_tot)`         | `r ncol(unemp_tot)`            |

| Number of rows of housing | Number of columns of housing |
|---------------------------|------------------------------|
| `r nrow(housing)`         | `r ncol(housing)`            |

| Number of rows of AAH | Number of columns of AAH |
|-----------------------|--------------------------|
| `r nrow(AAH)`         | `r ncol(AAH)`            |

| Number of rows of ASPA | Number of columns of ASPA |
|------------------------|---------------------------|
| `r nrow(ASPA)`         | `r ncol(ASPA)`            |

| Number of rows of ASS | Number of columns of ASS |
|-----------------------|--------------------------|
| `r nrow(ASS)`         | `r ncol(ASS)`            |

| Number of rows of PPA | Number of columns of PPA |
|-----------------------|--------------------------|
| `r nrow(PPA)`         | `r ncol(PPA)`            |

| Number of rows of RSA | Number of columns of RSA |
|-----------------------|--------------------------|
| `r nrow(RSA)`         | `r ncol(RSA)`            |

| Number of rows of france_serv | Number of columns of france_serv |
|-------------------------------|----------------------------------|
| `r nrow(france_serv)`         | `r ncol(france_serv)`            |

We notice that the number of rows and columns are almost always the same for these dataframes, because:

- we always study the 96 departments of metropolitan France, so the number of rows is always 96
- we always study the period 2015-2023 (or 2016-2023) so there are 8 or 9 years plus a column with the department number (which makes it 9 or 10 rows)

| Number of rows of bpe_clean | Number of columns of bpe_clean |
|-----------------------------|--------------------------------|
| `r nrow(bpe_clean)`         | `r ncol(bpe_clean)`            |

For the file of the BPE, the format is different:

- the number of rows is the number of departments times the numbers of facility type that we study
- the columns are the department code, the facility code, the facility name, and one column per year (2015, 2020, 2021, 2025).

We can also sum up the `clean_bpe` by representing the total number of structures for each facility type at the national level:

```{r}
#| echo: false 
#| label: tbl-bpe-totals
#| tbl-cap: "Number of facilities in metropolitan France, by year"

bpe_long |>
  group_by(`Facility Code`, `Facility Name`, year) |>
  summarise(total = sum(nb), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = total, names_sort = TRUE) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## Description of the key variables

The outcome variables that we are going to study are the unemployment rate and the poverty rate in each department.

The explanatory variables that we are going to use to understand the variations in these two outcome variables are: the number of social housing units, the number of beneficiaries of social minima, the number of France services houses and the number of facilites available in each department.

## Description of the data cleaning done

We started by importing the datasets that we had in our folders `Clean datasets` or `Raw datasets`. This step is done in the `Data import` section. We sometimes skipped some rows of the datasets that were empty rows of our Excel files.

Then we proceeded to the cleaning of the dataframes, in the `Data cleaning` section. Each dataframe had a unique structure, so the cleaning part really was specific to each of them. The usual actions we did were to `select` only the columns that were interesting for our study, `slice` out the rows that were not, and then `rename` the columns so they had coherent names.

For the poverty rates, we had to join all the annual dataframes so we could obtain a longitudinal one, where each row was a department and each column a year. The primary key we used to join was the department number (`dpt_id`).

## Research question

Since the mid-2010s, the physical presence of public services across French territories has been reorganised. Post offices have been closed or converted into lighter forms of service: municipal post offices run by town halls, and post office relays located in local shops. Between 2015 and 2025, the number of full post offices in metropolitan France fell by about a third, while relays and municipal post offices became more numerous. The network of public finance offices was restructured even more sharply, in particular with the “nouveau réseau de proximité” launched in 2019, which merged or closed many local tax and treasury offices. In parallel, the “France Services” one-stop shops were rolled out from 2020, partly to compensate for this retreat by gathering several administrations in a single place.

We ask whether departments where the local presence of public services declined more strongly experienced a different evolution of poverty, precariousness and access to housing than other departments. Our main target variable is the monetary poverty rate (INSEE, Filosofi). We complement it with two groups of indicators. Precariousness is measured by the number of recipients of minimum social benefits (RSA, AAH, minimum old-age pension ASPA, ASS) and of the in-work benefit (prime d’activité), relative to population. Access to housing is measured by the size of the social housing stock per inhabitant, which reflects the availability of affordable housing for low-income households.

We also explore, indirectly, one possible mechanism. When public services move further away or become less complete, people may claim fewer of the benefits they are entitled to, because procedures become harder to carry out without a nearby office (non take-up). No open data measure non take-up at the departmental level, so we cannot test this mechanism directly. However, if it is at work, departments losing more services should show a weaker increase in the number of benefit recipients than their evolution of poverty and unemployment would suggest. We therefore compare the evolution of benefit recipients with that of poverty, keeping in mind that this comparison only provides suggestive evidence.

We study the 96 departments of metropolitan France. Municipal data contain too many gaps because of statistical confidentiality, whereas departmental series are complete. Since departments are a small number of entities, we do a longitudinal analysis: each department is followed over time, and the analysis relies on changes within departments rather than on cross-sectional comparisons only. Public services are measured by the number of public finance offices, post offices, post office relays, municipal post offices and gendarmerie units per inhabitant, from INSEE’s Permanent Facilities Database (BPE). Since these harmonised counts are available for 2015, 2020, 2021 and 2025, we compare changes over 2015–2020 and 2015–2021, the periods for which all our outcome variables are also observed, and use 2025 to describe the later acceleration of closures. Outcomes are related to these changes over the same periods, with a one-year lag as a robustness check, controlling for unemployment and population.

Our results should be read as associations rather than causal effects. Departments that lose public services are often those that were already declining, through population loss or economic difficulties. We address this bias by controlling for initial levels and demographic trends, and we discuss it explicitly when interpreting the results.

## Graphical Representations

This section focuses on our main target variable, the poverty rate. We first map the poverty rate by department in 2021, using the department boundaries from IGN’s Admin Express COG (simplified version), to show where poverty is concentrated. We then map the change in the poverty rate between 2015 and 2021, in percentage points, to show where poverty increased, decreased or remained stable over the period.
We use 2021 rather than 2023 because the 2023 Filosofi data rely on a revised methodology and are not directly comparable with earlier years.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-poverty-map
#| fig-cap: "Poverty rate by department in 2021 (%). Sources: INSEE Filosofi; IGN Admin Express."

ggplot(map_data) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = `2021`), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#fde0dd", high = "#7a0177",
                      name = "Poverty rate (%)") +
  theme_void()

```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-poverty-change-map
#| fig-cap: "Change in the poverty rate by department between 2015 and 2021 (percentage points). Sources: INSEE Filosofi; IGN Admin Express."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6

change_labels <- c("Strong decrease (< -1.5 pts)",
                   "Decrease (-1.5 to -0.5 pts)",
                   "Stable (-0.5 to +0.5 pts)",
                   "Increase (> +0.5 pts)")

change_colours <- setNames(c("#2166ac", "#92c5de", "#bdbdbd", "#d6604d"),
                           change_labels)

map_change <- map_data |>
  mutate(change_class = cut(change,
                            breaks = c(-Inf, -1.5, -0.5, 0.5, Inf),
                            labels = change_labels))

ggplot(map_change) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = change_class), colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.15) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = change_colours, name = NULL,
                    drop = FALSE, na.value = "black") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        legend.text = element_text(size = 10))
```
